touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

# RESEARCH.md — git-a-profile Loop 1 (profile-researcher)

Working material for the Gate A decision. Do not commit this file.

---

## 1. Intake (verbatim)

- **Vibe:** "a heist crew with blueprints, ready for the heist" — planning-table energy, marked-up schematics, the crew, the job, go/no-go moments.
- **Must-haves:** the cost estimator (Loop 0a, `utils/cost-estimator.js`), the human gates (A/B/C), the PIIIX name, and **custom-designed tags/badges**.
- **Do-nots (absolute):** do NOT invent a logo for PIIIX or the project. A **hero banner is 100% required** (banner ≠ logo; wide scene-setting SVG is wanted).

---

## 2. Identity summary

`PIIIX-org/website-pitch-pipeline` is a docs-first operating system for an agent-run sales
pipeline: pick any geography, find local businesses with weak or missing websites, research
them into an Excel workbook, plan one bespoke site concept per business, build demo sites and
outreach emails, then file a mandatory run report to `runs/` on this repo. There is no
application code except one dependency-free Node script (the cost estimator). The product is
the *process*: six loop prompts you paste into Claude Code, three named human gates that stop
batch slop, a written 0–100 scoring rubric (≥90 to pass), a curated arsenal of external
skills/tools, and a hard legal section (public contacts only, source URLs, no invented
identities, demos honestly labeled as sales concepts).

Two truths matter for the concept work:

1. **The human is the lock on every door.** Gates A/B/C are described as non-negotiable and
   the docs repeat "quality collapses when agents batch without review."
2. **The crew works clean.** The legal/ethics rules are as load-bearing as the loops. Any
   heist framing has to be the *professional planning* kind, never the deception kind — the
   repo itself forbids dishonest positioning.

Also relevant: the previous README enhancement (commit `30e54f1`) was fully reverted
(`5ce1a55`, "restore README to pre-enhancement state for redo"). The reverted assets survive
in `assets/`: shields.io-style layouts, default indigo `#6366F1` palette, rounded-rect gate
badges, and `piiix-signature.svg` — a gradient circle mark that is exactly the invented-logo
move the do-nots now ban. That failed attempt is the baseline to beat.

Repo metadata is bare (no description, no topics, created 2026-07-23): the README carries the
entire first impression. Suggesting a repo description + topics is worth a note at Gate B/C,
out of scope here.

---

## 3. Sampled palette (hexes + sources)

**Source:** `https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/292071196?v=4` (PIIIX-org avatar, 460×460
PNG, downloaded to scratchpad as `piiix-avatar.png`, sampled with Pillow).

**It is a real logo, NOT a default identicon:** a charcoal field with an off-white ring and an
ornate monogram — a serif "I" crossed by four tapered arms forming a hexagonal silhouette,
wax-seal energy. (We may *reference* its geometry in layout rhythm; we must not redraw or
imitate the mark itself — that would be inventing/forking a logo.)

| Hex | Coverage | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `#272625` | 81.5% | Charcoal field — **brand anchor (dark)** |
| `#f5f9fb` | 16.7% | Porcelain white ring + monogram — **brand anchor (light)** |
| `#8e8f90` etc. | <0.5% | Anti-aliasing grays, ignore |

**Reconciliation with the heist/blueprint vibe:** the sampled charcoal + porcelain pair *is*
the night-job noir — chalk lines on slate. It anchors every scene. Blueprint cyanotype blue is
the **vibe layer**, used for paper/surfaces/linework inside illustrations, never as the brand
color. Proposed vibe hexes (cyanotype tradition, to be finalized in Loop 2):

- `#0E2A3F` cyanotype deep field · `#2E5C8A` blueprint mid · `#9CC3E0` blueprint linework
- One decision accent for go/no-go moments: stamp red `#B3402F` (HOLD) with porcelain `GO`
  lettering — a single warm accent so gate moments read instantly against all the cool tones.

Rule of thumb for Loop 2: charcoal/porcelain = the crew (frame, type, chrome); cyanotype = the
blueprints (scenes, diagrams); stamp red = the human's hand.

---

---
## 7. Concepts

### Concept 1 — "The Drawing Set"

**Pitch:** The README *is* the crew's numbered blueprint drawing set, assembled by their
draftsman. It opens on a wide cyanotype sheet (hero), then reads like flipping a bound set:
SHEET 00a (the takeoff/estimate), SHEET 00 (site prep), SHEETS 01–04 (the job), each carrying
a real blueprint title block. Between sheets sit inspection stamps — the human gates. Docs and
tools appear as the set's "schedules" (the way real drawings have door/window schedules). The
whole page reads top-to-bottom as: here are the drawings; nothing gets built past a sheet
until the inspector (you) stamps it.

- **Hero banner (wide SVG, no logos):** overhead planning-table scene — a large cyanotype
  sheet showing a storefront-website elevation with porcelain-pencil markup ("weak: no CTA",
  "mobile broken"), corner of a city grid map with pins labeled istanbul/berlin/nyc, a torn
  estimate slip showing real token numbers, one red inspection stamp mid-scene. Title block in
  the bottom-right corner of the *sheet* (not a logo): FIRM: PIIIX.org · DRAWN BY: agents ·
  CHECKED BY: **human** · SHEET 1 OF 7.
- **Custom tag/badge system — title-block stamps + revision clouds:** every doc/loop gets a
  miniature drawing title block (DWG NO · SHEET x/y · REV · CHECKED BY) instead of any pill.
  Repo lifecycle tags render as **revision clouds** (the scalloped bubbles drafters draw around
  changes) with the tag text inside. Gate approvals are dated rubber inspection stamps:
  "GATE A — PASSED — checked: HUMAN".
- **Loops/stages:** the sheet register — an SVG index panel listing SHEET 00a…04 with gate
  stamps drawn between rows; doubles as the state machine (candidate 1).
- **Docs/tools:** rendered as schedules — "MATERIALS SCHEDULE" (the ~40-tool arsenal grouped
  by loop, from the real Loop→tool matrix) and "SHEET REGISTER" (the file map, candidate 3).
- **Cost estimator:** SHEET 00a is literally the takeoff sheet — the real 12-model table drawn
  as an estimator's worksheet, 240× spread called out, "price the job before you take it."
- **Human gates:** the inspection stamps, the CHECKED BY line in every title block.
- **PIIIX:** the FIRM line of every title block + org description quoted as the firm's motto.
- **Category-reflex check:** "blueprint" is adjacent to the vibe words, but the load-bearing
  mechanic (title blocks, sheet register, revision clouds, schedules — real drafting
  conventions carrying real repo data) is not guessable from "heist README." Passes.
- **Accessibility note for later loops:** cyanotype linework needs contrast care
  (porcelain-on-`#0E2A3F` is fine; avoid mid-blue text on blue); no handwriting fonts for
  load-bearing text; every SVG needs meaningful alt text.

### Concept 2 — "Six Rooms, Three Doors"

**Pitch:** The README is the crew's walkthrough of the job site the night before. Hero shows a
wide isometric cutaway of a building — six rooms in sequence, a dashed route through them,
three locked doors on the route. Each README section then "enters" one room: the counting room
(0a), the prep room (0), the lookout (1), the drafting room (2), the workshop (3), the drop
(4). Doors A/B/C sit between rooms with keyholes drawn large; copy states plainly that agents
have no keys — only the human does. Tools live as kit laid out on each room's table. It ends
at the drop: the run report filed to `runs/`, "the job isn't done until the file exists."

- **Hero banner (wide SVG, no logos):** charcoal field, porcelain isometric linework of the
  six-room cutaway, cyanotype glow tracing the route, three doors with red HOLD lamps and one
  green-lit door being opened by a hand with a key. The name PIIIX appears only as stenciled
  plain type on the safehouse wall (typography, not a mark).
- **Custom tag/badge system — brass key tags / door plaques:** docs and tools get keyring fobs
  (hexagonal tags on a drawn ring — hexagonal to echo the avatar's silhouette rhythm without
  reproducing the monogram); rooms get engraved door plaques; repo lifecycle tags are keyring
  states (key cut → key in door → door open → outreach).
- **Loops/stages:** the cutaway map itself is the flow diagram; a slim linear "route card"
  version repeats it for screen readers and small screens.
- **Docs/tools:** per-room kit cards — "what's on the table in this room" — grouped exactly by
  the real Loop→tool matrix in TOOLS.md.
- **Cost estimator:** the counting room — you don't step onto the route until the job is
  priced; ledger-page SVG with the real model spread.
- **Human gates:** the three doors; the single strongest visual beat of the concept.
- **PIIIX:** stenciled name in the hero + "the crew works clean" section quoting the actual
  legal rules as the crew's code, signed PIIIX.org.
- **Category-reflex check:** "heist README" predicts corkboards, red string, masked crew
  member cards. This has none of those; an isometric architectural cutaway with a key/door
  system is a specific, drawable mechanic. Passes.
- **Accessibility note:** the isometric map is the riskiest asset in all three concepts — it
  must ship with the linear route-card fallback and thorough alt text, or it's hostile.
